title: Laparoscopic Nissen fundoplication
subtitle: Hiatal repair and 360 degree floppy wrap

sources.org: Society of American Gastrointestinal and Endoscopic Surgeons (SAGES)
sources.title: Guidelines for the surgical treatment of gastroesophageal reflux (GERD)

sources.org: Society of American Gastrointestinal and Endoscopic Surgeons (SAGES)
sources.title: Guidelines for the management of hiatal hernia

indications: Objectively proven gastro-oesophageal reflux disease with symptoms that persist despite adequate medical treatment, or in patients who do not wish to take long-term medication.
Reflux complications such as oesophagitis or stricture, and regurgitation that medication does not control.
Symptomatic sliding or para-oesophageal hiatal hernia requiring repair, where a fundoplication is added.
contraindications: Reflux not objectively proven: symptoms alone are not enough for an operation.
Achalasia or absent oesophageal peristalsis on manometry, where a full wrap causes severe dysphagia.
Unfit for general anaesthesia and pneumoperitoneum.
Severe obesity: a gastric bypass is often the better antireflux operation; discuss in a multidisciplinary setting.
Untreated major functional symptoms (for example gastroparesis or functional dyspepsia) that will persist after surgery.
preparation: Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy to assess oesophagitis, Barrett's oesophagus and the hiatus, and to exclude malignancy.
Ambulatory pH or pH-impedance monitoring off acid suppression where reflux is not already proven by severe oesophagitis.
High-resolution oesophageal manometry to exclude a motility disorder and guide the type of wrap.
Contrast swallow for large hiatal hernias or to define anatomy.

Consent must include dysphagia, gas bloat and inability to belch or vomit, increased flatulence, recurrence, wrap slippage or herniation, injury to the oesophagus, stomach, spleen, liver or vagus nerves, pneumothorax, conversion to open, and the possibility of a partial wrap instead.
positioning: Supine in steep reverse Trendelenburg, with legs apart (French position) or the surgeon on the patient's right, according to unit practice.
Secure the patient firmly with footplates or supports before tilting.
Arms out or tucked to allow the assistant and camera holder to stand comfortably.
equipment: Laparoscopic stack with a 30 or 45 degree telescope, five ports including a liver retractor port.
Energy device for the short gastric vessels.
Soft sling (for example a Penrose drain) for the oesophagus.
Non-absorbable sutures for crural repair and wrap, and a calibration bougie of the size the unit uses.
anatomy: The oesophageal hiatus is formed by the right crus of the diaphragm, which splits around the oesophagus; the aorta passes behind it through the aortic hiatus.
The anterior (left) vagus lies on the front of the oesophagus and the posterior (right) vagus behind it, usually separate from the oesophageal wall.
The phreno-oesophageal membrane anchors the oesophagus to the hiatus and is stretched in hiatal hernia.
The short gastric vessels connect the fundus to the spleen within the gastrosplenic ligament.
An accessory or replaced left hepatic artery may run in the lesser omentum.
The gastro-oesophageal junction lies beneath the fat pad; the angle of His lies between the fundus and the oesophagus.
criticalSafety: Identify and preserve both vagus nerves.
Obtain adequate intra-abdominal oesophageal length without tension.
Close the crura snugly but not tightly.
Pass the bougie only under vision and with explicit communication; stop at resistance.
Use the fundus for the wrap and keep it short and floppy.
Tell the anaesthetist if the pleura is opened, and watch for capnothorax.
structuresAtRisk: Liver and accessory left hepatic artery
commonErrors: Operating without objective proof of reflux.
Inadequate mediastinal mobilisation, leaving a short intra-abdominal oesophagus.
Wrap made from the body of the stomach, or around the stomach.
complications: Dysphagia, often early and temporary, sometimes persistent and requiring dilatation or revision.
Gas bloat, inability to belch or vomit, and increased flatulence.
Recurrent reflux, wrap slippage, disruption or herniation.
Oesophageal or gastric perforation, which may present late.
Vagal injury with delayed gastric emptying or diarrhoea.
postop: Prevent retching and vomiting with prophylactic antiemetics, because they can disrupt the wrap and the crural repair.
Start oral fluids early and progress to a soft diet as tolerated, avoiding bread and large solid boluses initially.
Stop acid suppression unless there is another indication, as advised by the unit.
Investigate fever, tachycardia, chest pain or new shortness of breath promptly: consider perforation or pneumothorax.
Follow up for dysphagia and reflux symptoms.

steps.emphasis: Confirm objective reflux evidence and manometry are in the notes; the type of wrap may change if motility is poor.
State the bougie size and who will pass it at the time-out.
Steep reverse Trendelenburg: the patient must be secured with footplates before the table is tilted.
Ports are placed high in the upper abdomen, aiming at the hiatus, with a separate port for the liver retractor.
Many surgeons divide the upper short gastric vessels to make a tension-free wrap; follow the unit's practice.
In a hiatal hernia, reduce the sac from the mediastinum and excise it from the junction, preserving the vagi.
Stop or convert for uncontrolled bleeding, suspected perforation, or anatomy at the hiatus you cannot define.
Inspect the spleen, the short gastric bed, the liver under the retractor and the hiatus at low pressure.
Record crural sutures, wrap type, length and calibration, and whether the pleura was breached.

step.nis.oesophageal-length.title: Mediastinal mobilisation and intra-abdominal oesophageal length
step.nis.oesophageal-length.why: A wrap placed under tension on a short oesophagus pulls up into the chest. Adequate intra-abdominal length, gained by mediastinal mobilisation, is one of the main protections against wrap herniation and recurrence.
how: With the sling around the oesophagus and vagi, dissect the oesophagus in the lower mediastinum circumferentially, keeping close to it and away from the pleura and aorta.
Aim for about 2 to 3 cm of tension-free intra-abdominal oesophagus with the gastro-oesophageal junction lying below the hiatus without traction.
Remove the gastro-oesophageal fat pad on the anterior surface, preserving the anterior vagus, to see the true junction.
If adequate length cannot be obtained after full mobilisation, stop and involve a senior surgeon: a lengthening procedure is a specialist decision.
pitfalls: Judging the junction position with traction on the sling, which overestimates the length.
Breaching the pleura and not telling the anaesthetist.
Mistaking the top of the stomach for the junction because the fat pad was left.

step.nis.wrap.title: Constructing a short, floppy 360 degree wrap
step.nis.wrap.why: The wrap restores a high-pressure zone at the gastro-oesophageal junction. A wrap that is too tight or too long causes dysphagia and gas bloat; a wrap made of the body of the stomach or placed below the junction slips and fails.
how: Pass the posterior fundus behind the oesophagus from left to right through the retro-oesophageal window, above the posterior vagus or including it with the oesophagus as your technique dictates.
Perform a 'shoe-shine' manoeuvre, moving the fundus back and forth behind the oesophagus, to confirm the correct part of the fundus is used and that it lies without tension or twist.

Approximate the two limbs of fundus anterior to the oesophagus over the calibration bougie with a few interrupted non-absorbable sutures, over a short length (commonly about 2 cm), incorporating a superficial bite of oesophageal wall in at least one to anchor the wrap.
Check that the wrap is loose enough for an instrument to pass between it and the oesophagus, lies above the junction, and that the anterior vagus is not caught.
Use a partial wrap (posterior or anterior) when manometry shows ineffective motility or the unit policy prefers it.
pitfalls: Using the body of the stomach instead of the fundus, producing a twisted, tight wrap.
Placing the wrap around the upper stomach rather than the oesophagus.
A long or tight wrap causing persistent dysphagia.
